strengths: The paper motivates multimodal planning clearly and presents an intuitive trajectory-vocabulary formulation for representing alternative driving actions.
VADv2 integrates camera-based perception, vectorized scene tokens, motion prediction, traffic-element modeling, and planning into a coherent end-to-end architecture.
The reported CARLA Town05 closed-loop results are strong, including an 85.1 Driving Score on Town05 Long and substantial improvements over the listed camera-only methods.
The study includes component ablations and qualitative examples illustrating multimodal trajectory proposals.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic-learning formulation is seriously underspecified. The paper never defines how pdata is constructed, how distance-dependent negative weights translate into a normalized target distribution, or whether/how the scalar scores p(a) are normalized. Consequently, the stated KL-divergence objective is not reproducible.

The claimed advantage over deterministic planning is not established experimentally. There is no matched deterministic regression baseline, and removing Distribution Loss also removes the primary expert-action supervision, so that ablation cannot isolate probabilistic modeling. No likelihood, calibration, mode-coverage, diversity, or ambiguity-focused evaluation is provided.

The novelty appears limited relative to established trajectory-anchor classification and multimodal trajectory prediction methods such as CoverNet and MultiPath. Calling the model a continuous probabilistic field is also questionable because training and inference operate primarily over 4,096 discrete vocabulary trajectories, with no evidence that probabilities generalize meaningfully to arbitrary continuous actions.

The inference description conflicts with some of the framing: the default policy selects the highest-probability action, which is deterministic rather than sampling, while the headline closed-loop results use an unspecified rule-based wrapper. The claimed stable fully end-to-end performance without that wrapper is not quantitatively reported.

The closed-loop evaluation lacks repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, per-infraction breakdowns, controlled reimplementations, and sufficient protocol details to determine whether comparisons taken from prior papers are directly comparable. Because CARLA results can be sensitive to routes, traffic configuration, simulator version, and wrapper design, the large gains are not adequately substantiated.

Ablations are restricted to open-loop displacement and collision metrics, which are known to correlate imperfectly with closed-loop driving. They do not study vocabulary size, sampling or decoding strategy, positional encoding, training-data scale, scene-conflict weighting, or comparison against alternative multimodal distributions such as mixtures.

Reproducibility is weak: loss coefficients, architecture dimensions, training schedule, target-generation procedure, conflict definitions, PID settings, rule-based wrapper, and computational requirements are omitted; the promised demonstration link is also blank.

The scope is limited to a single simulator benchmark, with training on CARLA's privileged autonomous agent and no real-world, cross-benchmark, robustness, or distribution-shift evaluation. Safety-relevant failure modes and the consequences of stochastic action selection are not analyzed.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: uncertainty and multimodality in end-to-end autonomous-driving planning.
The trajectory-vocabulary formulation is intuitive, and combining scene-token representations with conflict-aware supervision is practically motivated.
Reported camera-only closed-loop results on CARLA Town05 Long and Short are strong, including high route completion and driving scores.
The manuscript is generally readable, with a clear overview diagram and qualitative examples of multimodal trajectories.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty is substantially overstated. Discretizing trajectories into a vocabulary and predicting a categorical distribution closely resembles established trajectory-set classification and multimodal forecasting methods such as CoverNet and MultiPath. Calling this a continuous "probabilistic field" does not establish a materially new probabilistic formulation.

The central claim—that probabilistic planning handles uncertainty better than deterministic planning—is not directly tested. There is no controlled deterministic-regression baseline, mixture-density baseline, uncertainty/calibration evaluation, diversity metric, or analysis of genuinely ambiguous scenarios.

The method is underspecified. The paper does not precisely define the target data distribution, negative-sample weights, conflict loss, probability normalization, sampling procedure, trajectory horizon, architecture sizes, or many essential training details.

There is a conceptual inconsistency between repeatedly claiming that an action is sampled from the learned distribution and the inference section's use of the highest-probability action. Thus, the evaluated policy appears deterministic and does not validate the proposed sampling-based motivation.

The state-of-the-art comparison is not sufficiently controlled. Results are collected from prior papers with different sensors, training data, wrappers, and likely evaluation conditions; the paper provides no reproduced baselines, uncertainty across runs, per-route results, or statistical tests.

Closed-loop evaluation is limited to a single simulator benchmark and apparently uses an insufficiently specified rule-based wrapper. This makes it difficult to attribute performance gains to probabilistic planning rather than data scale, backbone design, auxiliary supervision, or wrapper behavior.

The ablations use only open-loop imitation metrics, which are known to correlate poorly with closed-loop driving. They omit the most important studies: vocabulary size, trajectory discretization, data scale, probability temperature/calibration, inference strategy, deterministic alternatives, and wrapper-free quantitative performance.

Several ablation differences are negligible, while the catastrophic result without distribution loss merely removes the primary behavioral supervision and provides little insight. No closed-loop evidence isolates the contribution of the proposed planning formulation.

Reproducibility is poor: optimizer and schedule, training duration and compute, camera configuration, image preprocessing, complete network specification, loss coefficients, PID settings, conflict thresholds, rule-based wrapper, and evaluation protocol are missing; no code or usable supplementary material is provided.
Safety claims are too strong for evidence obtained only in CARLA, and the paper lacks a substantive discussion of failure modes, distribution shift, rare events, or ethical and deployment risks.

strengths: The paper identifies an important problem: driving demonstrations can contain multiple valid actions, making deterministic trajectory regression unsuitable for genuinely multimodal situations.

The trajectory-vocabulary formulation is intuitive and integrates naturally with the vectorized scene representation, navigation information, and explicit agent, map, traffic-element, and image tokens.
The reported closed-loop CARLA results are strong. VADv2 achieves an 85.1 driving score on Town05 Long and 89.7 on Town05 Short using cameras only, substantially outperforming the listed methods.
The method is evaluated on both long and short routes, and the paper includes component ablations and qualitative examples of multimodal predictions.
The manuscript is concise, visually clear, and generally easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central claim about probabilistic planning is not convincingly isolated experimentally. There is no controlled deterministic-planning baseline with the same encoder, training data, capacity, auxiliary losses, and wrapper. Consequently, the large closed-loop improvement cannot be attributed specifically to probabilistic modeling.

The claimed action distribution is insufficiently defined. The paper does not specify the target distribution over vocabulary elements, its normalization, the negative-trajectory weights, or how the scalar outputs in Eq. 1 become a valid categorical distribution. Describing the loss as KL divergence is therefore not reproducible from the presented formulation.

Despite motivating the method through multimodality and uncertainty, the experiments do not measure distribution quality, calibration, mode coverage, diversity, likelihood, or performance specifically in ambiguous scenarios. The open-loop metrics evaluate only displacement and collision, and the qualitative results are not enough to validate the core uncertainty claim.

The closed-loop evidence lacks basic robustness information: the number of evaluation runs, random seeds, variance or confidence intervals, traffic settings, failure breakdowns, and statistical significance are not reported. CARLA scores can be sensitive to these factors.

Comparability is unclear because VADv2 uses approximately three million training frames, while training-data scale and conditions are not normalized across baselines. The rule-based wrapper and PID controller are also not specified, and no table reports closed-loop performance without the wrapper despite the paper emphasizing that capability.

The ablations are only open-loop, where improvements among most complete variants are extremely small. No closed-loop ablation establishes that the distribution loss, conflict loss, or 4096-element vocabulary drives the reported benchmark gain; vocabulary size, sampling strategy, and inference policy are not analyzed.

Important implementation details are absent, including the encoder and Transformer configuration, optimization schedule, trajectory horizon and timestamps, data balancing, loss coefficients, augmentation, compute requirements, and exact conflict-check construction. No code, trained models, or usable project link is provided, making reproduction difficult.

Evaluation is confined to two route sets from one simulator and does not test generalization to new simulator conditions, adverse weather, sensor corruption, rare events, or real-world datasets. Safety and deployment limitations receive little discussion. Overall, the promising benchmark result is not supported by sufficiently rigorous technical specification or controlled evidence for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: multimodal uncertainty in end-to-end autonomous-driving planning.
The trajectory-vocabulary approach is intuitive, computationally practical, and produces complete kinematically plausible trajectory primitives.
Reports strong closed-loop results across Town05, Bench2Drive, NAVSIM/NAVSIMv2, and a sizeable 3DGS-based benchmark.
Includes useful ablations on deterministic versus probabilistic planning, traffic density, vocabulary construction and size, training-set scale, scene tokens, and conflict supervision.
The architecture and experimental presentation are generally clear, with readable figures and tables.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic formulation is technically inconsistent. Equation 3 applies independent sigmoids, so outputs need not form a normalized distribution, yet Equations 4–5 treat them as one and invoke KL divergence/categorical cross-entropy.

The definition of pdata is unclear and potentially invalid: the paper says it is an occurrence frequency aggregated over all frames, which would be an unconditional marginal shared across scenes, while the claimed objective requires a scene-conditioned target—normally a per-sample one-hot or local soft distribution. The implementation cannot be reproduced from the description.

The conflict loss has a problematic sign: minimizing the stated sum of log p for conflicting actions is unbounded below as p approaches zero. A stable negative-label loss would normally use -log(1-p), or another bounded formulation. This further undermines technical soundness unless the equation differs from the implementation.

Novelty is limited relative to established anchor/vocabulary-based trajectory classification and multimodal planning. Calling the classifier a “probabilistic field” and drawing analogies to NeRF or language models do not establish a substantively new probabilistic methodology.

The decisive comparison only contrasts the method with a direct-regression head. There is no controlled comparison against conventional trajectory-anchor classification, mixture-density models, diffusion/flow planners, or a softmax version, so the source of the reported improvement is unresolved.

The multimodality experiment merely evaluates candidates ranked 1–5. It does not measure diversity, mode coverage, calibration, likelihood, uncertainty quality, or performance specifically on genuinely ambiguous scenes. Inference ultimately uses argmax, making the claimed benefit of learning a full distribution particularly unclear.

Closed-loop improvements are large despite nearly identical—and slightly worse—open-loop error and collision metrics versus deterministic planning. No repeated-run variance, statistical significance, route-level breakdown, or sufficiently detailed control-wrapper comparison is provided to substantiate this central result.

Comparability is uncertain because training data, perception backbones, modalities, wrappers, and data scale vary across baselines. The paper gives insufficient detail to verify that all headline comparisons isolate the planning contribution.

Reproducibility is weak: the abstract contains an empty code link; many training hyperparameters and loss weights are absent; the 2,000-hour dataset and 3DGS benchmark appear non-public; and real-vehicle evidence is deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

Safety-relevant deployment claims are stronger than the evidence. Evaluation remains simulation/reconstruction-based, and there is no uncertainty calibration, failure analysis, out-of-distribution study, or detailed treatment of real-world safety risks.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and presents a reasonably clear system architecture combining scene tokens with a discrete trajectory vocabulary.
The empirical scope is broad, covering Town05, Bench2Drive, NAVSIM/NAVSIMv2, and a 3DGS-based benchmark; several reported headline results are strong.
Ablations examine vocabulary size, data scale, token types, sampling strategies, and a deterministic trajectory-regression alternative.
weaknesses: The stated learning objective is fundamentally problematic. The model applies independent sigmoids rather than producing a normalized categorical distribution, while the distribution loss penalizes only the positive target. More seriously, the conflict loss is written as a positive sum of log p(a) and is minimized, making the objective unbounded below as conflicting-action probabilities approach zero. Consequently, the described optimization does not define a valid probabilistic model.

The central uncertainty claim is unsupported. Assigning each observation a single nearest-vocabulary trajectory and training with cross-entropy is standard anchor classification, not evidence that the conditional distribution of multiple reasonable actions has been learned. There are no likelihood, calibration, coverage, diversity, ambiguity-conditioned, or mode-recovery evaluations.

The description of the target distribution is internally inconsistent: it alternates between a one-hot label for each frame and an occurrence-frequency distribution aggregated over all frames. A global action-frequency distribution would not represent p(a|o), whereas one demonstration per observation does not directly identify that multimodal conditional distribution.

Inference selects the highest-probability trajectory, so the deployed policy remains deterministic. The comparison against direct regression does not isolate probabilistic modeling from trajectory discretization and architectural differences. Its large closed-loop advantage is reported without repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical testing, despite known variance in CARLA evaluation.

The paper claims operation without a rule-based wrapper, but the experimental protocol explicitly uses a TransFuser-like wrapper. This makes the headline closed-loop gains difficult to attribute to VADv2 and creates a direct contradiction in the presentation.

The custom 3DGS benchmark is insufficiently specified for independent validation: data, reconstruction procedure, metric implementation, baseline training, and evaluation protocol are not released or described adequately. Calling these experiments evidence of real-world effectiveness is too strong, since they remain simulation-based and are trained on 2,000 hours of proprietary demonstrations.

Baseline comparability is unclear because methods use different modalities, training data, backbones, wrappers, and possibly evaluation conditions. The manuscript gives no controlled reimplementation details for most headline comparisons and reports no variance across runs.

Furthest-trajectory sampling uses only endpoint distance, despite the claimed high-dimensional spatiotemporal action representation. Trajectories sharing an endpoint but following different paths can therefore be treated as equivalent, undermining action-space coverage and multimodality claims.

Reproducibility is poor: the abstract contains a blank code link; key architecture, optimization, loss-weighting, controller, wrapper, and dataset details are missing; and the claimed real-vehicle results are deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

Safety-related claims are overstated. The output scores are suggested as confidence values despite no calibration analysis, and the paper lacks an adequate discussion of deployment risks, distribution shift, failure cases, or safeguards for a safety-critical application.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant approach: discretizing full future trajectories into a large vocabulary and scoring them conditioned on vectorized scene tokens.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering Town05, Bench2Drive, NAVSIM/NAVSIMv2, and a photorealistic 3DGS-based benchmark, with particularly strong closed-loop results on Town05 Long and Bench2Drive.
The comparison against a deterministic trajectory-regression head provides useful evidence that the proposed formulation can improve closed-loop behavior, especially under higher traffic density.
Ablations examine major architectural components, vocabulary size, training-set scale, and vocabulary construction. The consistent gains with more data and finer vocabularies support the design.
Representing complete trajectories as tokens preserves demonstrated vehicle motion patterns and avoids the error accumulation associated with autoregressive waypoint generation.
The method remains camera-only and has reported latency comparable to the evaluated baselines, which strengthens its practical relevance.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic formulation is technically inconsistent. Equation 3 applies independent sigmoids rather than a normalized softmax, yet Equations 4–5 treat the outputs as a categorical probability distribution. Moreover, the conflict loss in Equation 6 minimizes log p for conflicting actions, which is unbounded below; a negative-label term such as -log(1-p) would normally be required. These issues make the stated objective mathematically unsound unless the implementation differs from the paper.

The claimed modeling of scene-conditioned multimodality is not convincingly evaluated. Table 6 only executes successively lower-ranked trajectories and shows decreasing performance; it does not measure mode coverage, diversity, calibration, conditional likelihood, or whether distinct valid behaviors are captured.

The description of pdata is ambiguous and partly contradictory: it is defined through dataset-wide occurrence frequencies, while training apparently uses a per-frame one-hot matched trajectory. A global marginal frequency would not represent the claimed scene-conditioned target distribution.

The novelty is moderate. Classification over trajectory anchors or vocabularies and multimodal trajectory prediction are established ideas, while the proposed “probabilistic field” appears operationally to be a transformer-based trajectory scorer over a fixed finite vocabulary.

Fairness and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. The paper lacks important training details and random-seed or variance reporting; Town05 comparisons may involve different training data and wrappers; and the rule-based wrapper is acknowledged but not specified or ablated. The promised code link is also missing.

Much of the real-world evidence relies on a private 2,000-hour training corpus and an internally constructed 3DGS benchmark. Dataset construction, splits, simulator dynamics, evaluation protocol, and baseline retraining details are limited, preventing independent verification. Claimed real-vehicle deployment results are deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

The 3DGS results are mixed rather than uniformly state of the art: although collision metrics improve, VADv2 is worse than some baselines on deviation and heading-related metrics. NAVSIM improvements over the strongest baselines are also relatively small.

The deterministic comparison changes the planning head to an MLP, so the large closed-loop gain does not cleanly isolate probabilistic training from differences in representation and model capacity. A controlled softmax-classification versus regression comparison, with matched architecture and compute, is needed.

Safety-relevant limitations are underdeveloped. The paper does not analyze rare failures, distribution shift, uncertainty calibration, intervention logic, or risks associated with deploying a sampled or top-ranked learned trajectory on real vehicles.
